title: Find a Suitable Home
tagline: Look for what an animal needs.
learningGoal: Use visible environmental clues to choose a suitable place for a pond fish or a tree squirrel, even when its appearance changes.
childTakeaway: I look for what the animal needs.
story: Pip is making a nature map. Help him look for water for a pond fish and useful trees for a tree squirrel. The animals stay safely in their own environments; choices are pictures for the map.
introPip: Help me make a nature map! Animals need places with things they use. We can look for those things.
conceptImageAlt: Pip stands beside a clear pond cutaway containing a submerged freshwater fish and aquatic plants. A gray tree squirrel holds an acorn on a branch beside a tree hollow.

ageSupport.entry: Start with two large picture choices and say the animal’s need in the question. A grown-up can read the prompt; the child may point or say an answer.
ageSupport.stretch: In round five, accept either suitable wooded scene and invite the child to point to a useful clue. Naming the other suitable scene is optional.

misconception: A matching color or a remembered background tells us where an animal belongs; each species has exactly one kind of home.

rounds.title: Water to swim
rounds.prompt: This pond fish needs water to swim. Which picture shows water?
rounds.sceneAlt: A pond fish icon above two equally framed pictures: a pond with water and aquatic plants on the left; a dry grassy patch on the right.
rounds.success: The pond has water. Our pond fish swims in water.
hints: Imagine the fish swimming. Which picture gives it water around its body?
The left picture is a pond. It has water for our pond fish.
rounds.visualHint: Only after a hint, trace the pond water boundary and animate a separate demonstration fish swimming fully underwater. Do not show a fish flopping on land.
rounds.whyThisRound: Establishes a need-based choice with a stated need and an obvious environmental difference.

rounds.title: Trees to use
rounds.prompt: This tree squirrel climbs trees. Which picture has trees to climb?
rounds.sceneAlt: A gray tree squirrel icon above two equally framed pictures: open pond water with aquatic plants on the left; a wooded park with trees, hollows and acorns on the right.
rounds.success: The wooded park has trees to climb. A tree squirrel can use the branches and shelter in a hollow or nest.
hints: Trace a trunk up to a branch. Is it in the pond picture or the park picture?
The right picture has trees. This tree squirrel can climb them.
rounds.visualHint: Trace a tree trunk to its branch, then show a separate squirrel climbing it. Make the hollow visible; do not imply water is useless to squirrels.
rounds.whyThisRound: Introduces a second animal and a different useful environmental feature.

rounds.title: Color does not choose the home
rounds.prompt: This pond fish is brown. Which place has water for it to swim?
rounds.sceneAlt: A brown pond fish icon above two equally framed pictures: dry brown sand on the left; a blue pond with water and aquatic plants on the right.
rounds.success: The blue pond has water. The fish’s brown color does not change its need for water.
hints: Look for what the fish needs, even if the colors are different.
Picture the brown fish swimming. Sand is dry; the pond is full of water.
Choose the blue pond on the right. The brown fish still needs water.
rounds.visualHint: Show brown and golden demonstration fish swimming in the same pond. Do not use crossed-out color patches as the explanation.
rounds.whyThisRound: Checks whether the child uses a need rather than matching the fish’s color.

rounds.title: Find both useful clues
rounds.prompt: This tree squirrel uses trees to climb and nuts for food. Which picture shows both trees and nuts?
rounds.sceneAlt: A dark tree squirrel icon above three equally framed pictures: acorns on open grassy ground on the left; trees, hollow shelter and acorns in the middle; trees without pictured acorns on the right.

choices.label: Trees without pictured nuts
choices.spokenLabel: Trees with no nuts in the picture

rounds.success: The middle picture shows both trees and nuts. It shows places to climb and food to eat.
hints: Look for two things: trees and nuts.
Point to a tree. Now look for nuts in that same picture.
The middle picture shows trees and nuts together. The other pictures show just one of those clues.
rounds.visualHint: After a hint, reveal two simple tokens for a tree and an acorn, then gently outline each corresponding clue in the middle scene. These tokens are an explanation, not a hidden requirement before the prompt.
rounds.whyThisRound: Transfers from one clue to two visible needs, while carefully asking about the picture rather than declaring every tree-only scene unsuitable.

rounds.title: More than one place can work
rounds.prompt: Choose one place with trees, shelter, and nuts for our tree squirrel.
rounds.sceneAlt: A tree squirrel icon above three equally framed pictures: a woodland with hollow trees, nuts and a small water patch on the left; a bare paved courtyard in the middle; a wooded park with hollow trees, nuts and a small water patch on the right.
rounds.success: Either wooded picture works. Both show trees, shelter, and nuts. An animal can have more than one suitable place.
hints: Look for places to climb, a hollow for shelter, and nuts.
Point to those things in a picture. You may notice them in more than one picture.
The woodland on the left and the wooded park on the right both show those things. You can choose either one.
rounds.visualHint: After the child chooses or asks for help, show the same clue tokens beside both wooded scenes with equal treatment. Each is an accepted single choice.
rounds.whyThisRound: Optional stretch checks needs across two changed environments and explicitly avoids the one-species-one-home misconception.

finale: Pip’s nature map now shows useful pond and woodland places. The fish swims under water; the tree squirrel explores branches. Pip says, “We looked for what each animal uses!”
offlineActivity: With a grown-up, draw a pond fish and a tree squirrel. Add water around the fish; add trees, shelter, and food around the squirrel. Ask, “What did you add that helps this animal?” Use drawings rather than moving or feeding wildlife.
reviewQuestions: Should the first version stay with these two animals so the child can learn a reasoning pattern before adding more species?
Is the two-clue question in round four clear enough, or should we keep one visible need per question until child playtesting?
Should the optional final round accept either wooded picture with a single tap, and then invite an explanation without requiring speech?
designNotes: This is an adult review concept, not a tested child experience. The diagrams and exact prompts are the instructional authority; the generated concept image is story art.

The pictured fish represents a freshwater pond fish, informed by bluegill habitat examples. Do not generalize that every fish can live in any pond or that visually blue water proves suitable water quality.

The squirrel is a tree squirrel, informed by eastern gray squirrel references. Ground squirrels and other species may have different habitat needs. Trees, acorns, and hollows are useful visible clues, not a complete ecological checklist.
Round four asks which picture visibly shows both trees and nuts. It does not declare a tree-only landscape an impossible habitat: food may exist beyond the pictured area.
Round five accepts either woodland or wooded park. The child need not select both or find a hidden preferred answer.
No amphibians are used as exclusive land-versus-water distractors. If later adding frogs or turtles, recognize their use of both environments and research the named species.
These scenes do not ask children to release pets, move animals, or feed wildlife. The nature map provides the story action.
The target duration and age supports are design estimates requiring child observation, not developmental certification.

sources.title: Minnesota DNR — MinnAqua: Design a Habitat
sources.supports: Pages 4–5 explain food, water, cover, and space; bluegills can use the quieter water of many lakes and ponds. Fish species have different water conditions and habitat needs. This reference informs scientific content; its core lesson targets grades 3–5, so it does not validate this age adaptation.

sources.title: National Park Service — Eastern Grey Squirrel, Lowell
sources.supports: Eastern gray squirrels use woodland and urban parks; their diet includes nuts, acorns, seeds, and berries. More than one environmental setting can support the same species.

sources.title: Minnesota DNR — Gray squirrel
sources.supports: Gray squirrels use hardwood forests, wooded parks and residential areas. Acorns and other tree seeds are foods; shelter may be a tree hollow or a leafy tree-top nest.
